items.title: Just 23 people give a 50/50 chance of a shared birthday
items.claim: How many people do you need in a room for it to be more likely than not that two share a birthday? Most people guess 100 or 180. The answer is 23.
items.prompt: Why is the threshold so low?

options.text: With 23 people there are 23 choose 2 = 253 possible pairs, each with about a 1/365 chance of matching; the question is not 'matches me' but 'any match anywhere', which has many more chances
Coincidences happen because of cosmic alignment

items.reveal:
The probability that NO two people in a group of n share a birthday is (365/365)(364/365)(363/365)...((365-n+1)/365).

For n = 23, this product equals about 0.493. Probability of AT LEAST ONE match equals 1 - 0.493 = 0.507. Just over 50 percent.
For n = 41, probability of a match is about 90 percent.
For n = 70, about 99.9 percent.

Intuition fails because we ask 'does someone share MY birthday?' — that requires n ≈ 253 for 50 percent. The real question allows ANY pair to match, and the number of pairs grows as n choose 2 ≈ n squared / 2.

This 'birthday attack' is important in cryptography: collision resistance of a hash function with N possible outputs only protects against attackers who try fewer than about square root of N inputs. A 128-bit hash gives only 64-bit collision security.
items.why: Counting pairs is qualitatively different from counting people. Pair counts grow quadratically, so coincidences are far more likely than a head-count suggests.

items.title: Some quadratics never touch zero — and you can prove it in one step
items.claim: x^2 + 2x + 5: positive for every real x. The graph never reaches zero. You don't need calculus or graph-plotting — you can see this in one rearrangement.

options.text: Complete the square: x^2 + 2x + 5 = (x + 1)^2 + 4. The first term is non-negative; adding 4 means the whole expression is at least 4. Never zero
It cannot be proved without calculus

items.reveal:
For ax^2 + bx + c with a > 0, the discriminant b^2 - 4ac determines:
- Discriminant > 0: two real roots; graph crosses x-axis twice.
- Discriminant = 0: one repeated real root; graph touches x-axis.
- Discriminant < 0: no real roots; graph stays entirely above x-axis (if a > 0) or below (if a < 0).

x^2 + 2x + 5: a = 1, b = 2, c = 5. Discriminant = 4 - 20 = -16 < 0. No real roots.

Completing the square gives a stronger statement: the MINIMUM value of the quadratic. (x + 1)^2 + 4 has minimum 4 when x = -1. So x^2 + 2x + 5 is always at least 4.

General quadratic ax^2 + bx + c = a(x + b/(2a))^2 + (c - b^2/(4a)). Minimum value (for a > 0) is c - b^2/(4a) = -(b^2 - 4ac)/(4a) — same expression as the discriminant.

Applications:
- Optimisation: many minimisation problems reduce to completing the square.
- Inequality proofs: AM-GM and Cauchy-Schwarz often pivot on quadratic positivity.
- Definite matrices: a quadratic form x^T M x > 0 for all non-zero x means M is positive definite — central to optimisation and statistics.
items.why: Quadratics feel like they should always cross zero somewhere. Many don't. The discriminant settles which ones, and completing the square exposes the minimum directly — without calculus.

items.title: You cannot walk across all seven Königsberg bridges once
items.claim: Königsberg (now Kaliningrad) sat on two riverbanks and two islands connected by seven bridges. The town's puzzle: is there a route that crosses each bridge exactly once? Euler proved in 1735 that there isn't — and invented graph theory in the process.
items.prompt: What's the criterion for the puzzle to have a solution?

options.text: Bridges must be arranged in a circle
Every vertex (landmass) must have even degree (an even number of bridges), except possibly the start and end points; Königsberg has four landmasses, all of odd degree
Bridges must be the same length

items.reveal_title: Euler's 1735 paper — birth of graph theory
items.reveal:
Euler abstracted Königsberg to a 'graph': landmasses become vertices, bridges become edges. The puzzle asks for an 'Eulerian path' (a walk using every edge exactly once).

Euler proved: an Eulerian path exists if and only if at most 2 vertices have odd degree. (A circuit, starting and ending at the same vertex, requires every vertex to have even degree.)

Königsberg: north bank had 3 bridges, south bank 3, east island 5, west island 3. All four are odd. So no Eulerian path exists.

Euler's paper was the first to study a problem in what we now call topology — caring about connections, not distances. Graph theory grew into a major branch of mathematics: shortest paths, network flows, Internet routing, social networks, and more.

Two of Königsberg's bridges were destroyed in World War II; only three of the original seven remain. Today the puzzle has a valid Eulerian path.
items.why: Geometric puzzles often look like they need detailed measurement. Sometimes only the abstract topology matters — and Euler's degree condition makes the answer trivial once formalised.
